title: India's Trade Deficit Just Blew Past Forecasts. The Hormuz Crisis Is Now Showing Up in the Numbers.
excerpt: Exports fell to $40.4 billion in June as shipping disruptions in the strait choked Indian trade. The $30.4 billion gap is almost $4 billion worse than economists expected — and remittance math is getting harder.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's trade deficit widened to $30.43 billion in June, exceeding forecasts by nearly $4 billion.
  • Merchandise exports dropped nearly 11% to $40.41 billion, while imports fell to $70.84 billion.
  • Services exports remained strong at $33.03 billion, yielding a services trade surplus of $15.11 billion.
  • The rupee weakened to 95.62 per dollar, influenced by rising oil prices and trade deficit concerns.
  • Goldman Sachs predicts the Reserve Bank of India will raise interest rates by 25 basis points in upcoming months.

India's merchandise trade deficit widened sharply to $30.43 billion in June, government data released on Monday showed, blowing past economists' expectations of $26.63 billion as exports fell faster than imports amid crippling shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. The gap — up from $28.21 billion in May — is the clearest evidence yet that the Iran war's chokehold on the world's most critical waterway is now extracting a measurable toll on India's economy. ## The Numbers Tell a Story of Disruption Merchandise exports dropped to $40.41 billion in June from $45.2 billion the previous month — a decline of nearly eleven per cent in a single month. Imports fell too, but less sharply, to $70.84 billion from $73.41 billion. The pattern is familiar to trade economists: when a major shipping lane goes dark, both sides of the ledger shrink, but exports — which depend on competitive freight rates and predictable delivery windows — suffer more. India's exporters, particularly small and medium businesses that account for nearly half the country's outbound shipments, have been rerouting cargo around the Cape of Good Hope or absorbing ballooning war-risk insurance premiums since the Strait of Hormuz closures began. Freight costs on some Gulf routes have tripled. "This is what disruption looks like in the data," a senior trade ministry official said. "It is not that demand has collapsed — it is that the cost and complexity of moving goods has fundamentally changed." ## A Bright Spot Buried in the Wreckage Not everything in the trade data is bleak. For the full April-to-June quarter, India's goods exports actually rose about fifteen per cent from a year earlier, buoyed by pricier petroleum shipments and strong demand from non-Gulf markets. Services exports remained robust at $33.03 billion in June, with services imports at $17.92 billion — yielding a healthy services trade surplus of $15.11 billion that partially offsets the goods gap. India's trade secretary, Rajesh Agrawal, struck an upbeat note on the broader trajectory, saying the bilateral trade agreement with the United States was progressing "well" and that the framework deal was ready. "Whenever it is the right time, it will be signed," he said. But that optimism sits uneasily next to the June data. India recently walked away from a quick trade deal with Washington, holding out for better terms — a gamble that looks riskier when your trade deficit is running nearly four billion dollars above expectations. ## Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention For the nine million Indians living in the Gulf and the millions more who send money home from the United States, Canada, and Britain, the widening trade gap is not an abstraction. It feeds directly into the rupee's trajectory. The rupee slid to 95.62 per dollar on Monday — its weakest level in over a month — as oil prices rose three per cent on the latest Hormuz escalation. Options markets now show a clear bearish bias on the currency, with traders betting on further depreciation. A weaker rupee means every dollar, pound, or dirham sent home buys more in nominal terms — but it also signals deeper stress in India's external accounts. If oil prices stay elevated and exports keep falling, the Reserve Bank of India may be forced to hike interest rates, which would slow the domestic economy and dent the stock market gains that have drawn diaspora investment. Goldman Sachs analysts expect the RBI to raise rates by twenty-five basis points in both October and December. Swap markets are pricing in a similar trajectory.

## The Strait That Controls Everything The trade data lands on the same day that President Donald Trump declared the United States the "Guardian of the Hormuz Strait" and proposed charging a twenty per cent toll on all cargo shipped through — a proposal the United Nations shipping agency immediately rejected as having no legal basis. For India, which imports over eighty per cent of its crude oil and sixty per cent of its cooking gas through Gulf routes, the strait's status is not a geopolitical abstraction. It is the single most important variable in the country's economic outlook. India's retail inflation also breached the central bank's four per cent target for the first time in seventeen months on Monday, hitting 4.38 per cent in June — driven in large part by higher fuel and food costs linked to the war. The monsoon, which brings seventy per cent of India's annual rainfall, is running eighteen per cent below average, threatening crop production and adding another layer of price pressure. ## What Comes Next The immediate question is whether the Hormuz disruption is temporary or structural. If the U.S. blockade on Iranian shipping takes effect as announced — at 2000 GMT on Tuesday — and Iran continues to attack vessels in the strait, Indian exporters face months of elevated costs and delays. India's emergency oil stockpile approval last week and its push to diversify energy sources through new partnerships with Russia, Saudi Arabia via alternative routes, and domestic production signal that New Delhi is preparing for a prolonged disruption.
Economic Impact of the Hormuz Crisis
›Rupee weakened to 95.62 per dollar.
›Oil prices rose by 3% amid tensions.
›Retail inflation hit 4.38%, breaching target.
›Goldman Sachs expects RBI rate hikes.
For diaspora investors and remitters, the next data points to watch are wholesale inflation on Tuesday, the RBI's next policy statement, and any resolution — or further escalation — in the Hormuz standoff. The trade numbers do not lie. The war is in the data now.
